nameStory: The hackberry emperor gets its royal name from its close relationship with hackberry trees, where it spends its entire life cycle from egg to adult. Like an emperor ruling over its domain, this butterfly is completely dependent on hackberry trees as its sole host plant, making it the undisputed monarch of the hackberry kingdom.
description: The hackberry emperor is a medium-sized butterfly with brownish-orange wings marked by distinctive dark spots and eyespots. As a member of the brush-footed butterfly family, it has shortened front legs that look almost like little brushes. These quick, darting butterflies are unusual because they rarely visit flowers, instead preferring to feed on tree sap, rotting fruit, and even animal droppings for their nutrients.

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Look for brownish-orange wings with a series of dark spots and prominent eyespots along the wing edges that feel papery to the touch when handled

idTips.label: Flight behavior
idTips.description: Watch for quick, mercurial flight patterns with sudden stops and starts, often darting around hackberry trees rather than floating like many other butterflies

idTips.label: Feeding habits
idTips.description: Notice they avoid flowers entirely, instead clustering around tree wounds with sticky sap, overripe fruit with a sweet fermenting smell, or fresh animal scat

idTips.label: Brush-like front legs
idTips.description: The shortened front legs are held close to the body like tiny brushes and feel fuzzy when observed up close

idTips.label: Hackberry association
idTips.description: Always found near hackberry trees with their distinctive warty bark texture and small berry-like fruits in late summer

habitat: Look for hackberry emperors in lowlands and areas near water sources where hackberry trees thrive, including river valleys, floodplains, and moist woodland edges. They're often found in parks, suburban areas, and disturbed sites where hackberry trees have colonized. The butterflies stay close to their host trees, rarely wandering far from hackberry groves.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with fresh individuals showing bright, unmarked wings as they seek mates around hackberry trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in summer when adults are most abundant, laying clustered eggs on hackberry leaves and engaging in territorial behavior.
seasonality.fall: Late-season adults may appear more worn and faded, while larvae feed on hackberry foliage before overwintering as caterpillars.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity; larvae overwinter in hackberry bark crevices or leaf litter, waiting for spring warmth to resume development.

funFact: Hackberry emperors are basically butterfly 'cheaters' — they steal nectar from flowers without pollinating them, making them parasites rather than the helpful pollinators we usually expect butterflies to be!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative the tawny emperor, but hackberry emperors have more distinct eyespots and darker markings. Memory trick: 'Hackberry has more hack marks' — the hackberry emperor shows more contrasting dark spots and defined patterns than the more uniformly tawny-colored tawny emperor.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'emperors,' these butterflies are actually quite dependent and specialized, unable to survive without their single host plant species. This makes them vulnerable to habitat loss when hackberry trees are removed from landscapes.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative the tawny emperor, the hackberry emperor displays more pronounced eyespots and sharper contrast between light and dark wing markings. While both species depend on hackberry trees, hackberry emperors tend to have more defined wing patterns with clearer spotting, whereas tawny emperors appear more uniformly colored with subtler markings throughout their wings.
